extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on writing and evaluating novels, focusing on characterization, point of view, and plot construction with illustrative examples from major novelists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of a round character
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way. If it never surprises, it is flat. If it does not convince, it is a flat pretending to be round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round characters have 'the incalculability of life about them' and may sometimes be used alone but more often in combination with flat characters to achieve acclimatization and harmony in a novel. Examples: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky characters, Madame Bovary, Becky and Beatrix (Thackeray), Parson Adams, Tom Jones. Anti-pattern: characters labeled by a single quality and never surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters: economy and recognizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters appear simple and never need re-introduction; they are useful when they reliably represent particular types or qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat figures (e.g., Henry Tilney, Mr. Woodhouse, Charlotte Lucas) can be labelled 'Sense', 'Pride', etc., yet should not be tethered to only those qualities. Use flat characters to support the novel by providing familiar, stable elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view options and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist can describe characters from outside (impartial/partial onlooker), assume omniscience (describe from within), place the narrator as one of the characters (limited/ignorant of others' motives), or adopt intermediate attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different points of view produce different technical problems. Examples: Dickens's shifting POV in Bleak House (omniscient → partial omniscience → dramatic/inhabiting a character), Gide's Les Faux Monnayeurs (sophisticated attention to jolts), Tolstoy's shifts which 'come off'. Choose the POV that can 'bounce' readers into acceptance; avoid methodological ostentation that draws attention to the author rather than the characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to 'bounce' the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist must have the power to 'bounce' the reader into accepting what he says; this is central to the aesthetics of fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to shift viewpoint or register (omniscient, partial, dramatic) is acceptable provided the writer can make readers accept these shifts. Dickens and Tolstoy demonstrate successful bouncing; Lubbock places point of view at the centre of method but the essayist locates the central power in the writer's ability to bounce readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of authorial intimacy about characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should not take the reader into his confidence about individual characters; such intimacy usually harms illusion and nobility and leads to facetiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial confidences about individuals invite bar-parlour chattiness ('Doesn't A look nice — she always was my favourite'), cool the creative state, and divert the reader to examine the novelist's mind. It is less dangerous to generalize about the universe than about individuals. Fielding and Thackeray's intimacy is cited as damaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege to portray the secret life and subconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist has access to characters' secret life and subconscious; this is a unique privilege of the novel and must not be surrendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelist can show self-communings, subconscious short-circuiting into action, and soliloquy. Critics who ask 'How did the writer know that?' mistake the court-like insistence on fixed standpoint for what matters; what matters is whether the depiction is convincing (troavov).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of plot (causality over sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot is a narrative of events in which the emphasis falls on causality rather than mere time-sequence. (Contrast: 'The king died and then the queen died' (story) vs 'The queen died of grief at the king's death' (plot)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot suspends the time-sequence and asks 'why?' Plot is a form capable of high development (mystery, cause-and-effect). It cannot be reduced to mere 'and then — and then'; it demands intelligence and memory from the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot requires intelligence and memory from the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: To grasp a plot, the reader must have intelligence (to hold and relate facts) and memory (to retain earlier facts so causes and effects connect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intelligent reader sees facts both in isolation and in relation to previous pages; memory prevents loose ends. Plot-makers expect readers to remember; writers should leave no loose ends and avoid misleading. Examples: highly organized novels like The Egoist where facts form cross-correspondences revealed properly only at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and organic unity in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action or word ought to count; plot ought to be economical and spare, organic and free from dead matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when complicated, a good plot should not mislead. As the plot unfolds, the reader's memory rearranges clues into chains of cause and effect; a fine plot yields an aesthetically compact final sense that could not have been shown outright without losing beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery as essential to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery (the 'detective element')—a suspension of the time-sequence or a pocket in time—is essential to a plot and cannot be appreciated without intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystery ranges from crude ('Why did the queen die?') to subtle (half-explained gestures whose meaning dawns later). To appreciate mystery part of the mind must brood while another goes on; curiosity alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should produce convincing surprises
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot ought to cause surprise; when the incident shocks yet afterwards seems 'all right', it signals a well-constructed plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Meredith's contrivances (horse-whipping of Dr. Shrapnel) — shocks that transform characters and their world. A successful shock reacts upon characters and alters them; the plot's surprises should feel organic to character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between plot and character autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid subordinating characters wholly to the plot; characters should retain vitality and not be forced to suspend their natures at every turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When plot triumphs too completely, characters become weakened, 'dry and thin' (a criticism applied to Hardy's novels except Tess). Meredith knew where the plot could demand a contribution and where to let characters function freely. The novelist must not canalize human happiness and misery solely into action (contrary to Aristotle's view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not have a character violate an established moral or narrative obligation (e.g., a narrator who has pledged to tell everything but then suppresses knowledge) without cost to credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In Villette Lucy Snowe conceals a discovery; the resulting plot thrill comes at the expense of perceived integrity. Such concealment may be trivial or harmful, but it risks distressing the reader's trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive authorial self-analysis about method
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist who betrays too much interest in his own method (summoning readers to analyse his mind) becomes merely 'interesting' rather than 'vital'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gide's Les Faux Monnayeurs is sophisticated about jolts and method; overattention to method leads to a drop in emotional temperature and loss of character creation. Writers should not invite readers into examining the novelist's mind at the cost of the fiction's immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit excessive brooding by characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must not brood too long or waste time in inward ladders; they should at some point contribute to the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot (visualized as a higher government official) may reproach characters that overstep limits; while individuality is valuable, a novel requires characters to contribute or risk jeopardizing higher interests of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems with denouement: preserve character life at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels are often feeble at the end because the plot requires winding up, causing characters to go 'dead' as the author forces them to contribute to the denouement (commonly by death or marriage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inherent defect is due partly to failure of pep and partly to earlier character independence. The writer must manage endings to avoid reducing final impressions to 'deadness' and over-reliance on conventional closures (death/marriage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow organic growth vs over-planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether the novel must be planned in advance; consider allowing the novel to grow and carry the writer to unforeseen goals instead of rigid predetermination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern writers experiment with replacing classical plot structures (complication, crisis, solution) with alternative frameworks. Gide's novel contains both planned plot fragments and more open, caboodle-like interplays (diary, impressions). Decide when to stand above the work (plot-maker) and when to throw oneself into it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty in plot should emerge, not be directly aimed for
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty may be part of a completed plot; a novelist should not aim directly at beauty though he fails if he does not achieve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty in plot appears as an aesthetically compact final sense that surprises; it ought to look 'a little surprised' rather than prima-donna self-assuredness. The author should design for effect without obviously telegraphing the pursuit of beauty.
